item.title: Impact of Negative Weights on Performance in Reservoir Computing
item.description: arXiv:2611.06051v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Reservoir computing provides an efficient framework for time-series prediction because only the readout layer is trained while the recurrent reservoir remains fixed. In this study, we examine how the negative sign ratio of a signed Erdos-Renyi reservoir affects the internal dynamics and forecasting performance of an echo state network on the Mackey-Glass benchmark. To characterize the reservoir responses, we use two Shannon-entropy-based observables, namely node-state entropy and node-frequency entropy, as empirical proxies for the diversity of reservoir states and temporal activation patterns. We find that intermediate negative sign ratios are associated with richer internal dynamics and substantially lower prediction error than the sign-homogeneous extremes for the task considered here. These results suggest that link-sign composition can be a useful structural parameter in reservoir design for chaotic forecasting. The present findings should be interpreted within the scope of the current benchmark and reservoir setting, and broader validation will be required to establish their generality across other tasks, topologies, and controlled spectral conditions.
item.dc:creator: Yeonsu Jeong, Seonho Nam, Dahan Choi, Mi Jin Lee, Seung-Woo Son

item.title: Temporary gas turbines powering a US AI data center created a cross-state air pollution hotspot
item.description: arXiv:2611.06115v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Data centers increasingly use on-site gas turbines that regulators can treat as temporary. Two satellites show the fleet powering SpaceXAI's Colossus 2 raised local nitrogen dioxide columns by about half as it expanded, the most anomalous increase among 656 urban locations nationwide since 2020. Mississippi authorized the fleet, but two-thirds of the hotspot's 116,000 mostly Black residents live in Tennessee, and the hotspot contains no regulatory nitrogen dioxide monitor. The fleet causes an estimated four premature deaths yearly, valued at $49 million, over 80% outside Mississippi and nearly all from units without selective catalytic reduction. On new turbines, this control's benefits exceed costs over the service life, but not over temporary stays or for in-state damages alone. Standards following the equipment could recover these benefits.
item.dc:creator: Will W. Qiang, Bo Huang, Xingjian Liu, Harry F. Lee

item.title: AGORA cities: the hidden infrastructure shaping urban fragility
item.description: arXiv:2611.06289v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Urban services are unevenly distributed across the city, yet it is unclear when their joint presence signals fragility and when it instead outlines a neighbourhood's vocation. For Bologna and Florence, we integrate Foursquare and OpenStreetMap points of interest with Sentinel-2-derived green indicators based on the 3-30-300 rule, cluster urban areas accordingly, and benchmark the clusters against the demographic, social, economic and composite fragility indices produced by the municipal statistical offices, which are exogenous to the analysis. In both cities, we identify a subset of infrastructures, termed AGORA (Arts, Green environments, and Open Routes for Access and mobility), whose joint provision is associated with lower fragility. The AGORA Alignment score (AA), based on the rank correlation between AGORA endowment and composite fragility, indicates full alignment in Florence (AA = 1.00) and strong but incomplete alignment in Bologna (AA = 0.80). The remaining service categories instead show wide and heterogeneous distributions: they differentiate areas without tracking fragility and can be interpreted as expressions of urban vocations. The least fragile cluster, the only one with full AGORA endowment, hosts just 3.3% of residents in Bologna and 6.3% in Florence. The framework offers a procedure transferable to other contexts and identifies the expansion of AGORA infrastructures as a candidate lever for reducing fragility without altering existing vocations.
item.dc:creator: Eleonora Andreotti, Munazza Usmani, Alice Barsanti, Maurizio Napolitano

item.title: Stochastic dose fluctuations in boron neutron capture therapy with heterogeneous boron distributions
item.description: arXiv:2611.06344v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Dose fluctuations at the cellular scale in boron neutron capture therapy (BNCT) arise from stochastic neutron capture and spatially heterogeneous boron distributions. This study develops a stochastic framework combining energy-deposition responses from Geant4 simulations, a Poisson capture process, and spatially correlated lognormal boron fields to investigate nuclear dose variance and zero-hit probability. The results show that the variance contribution from stochastic neutron capture increases linearly with neutron fluence, whereas the contribution from boron heterogeneity increases quadratically. These distinct scaling behaviors produce a correlation-length-dependent crossover between the dominant sources of dose fluctuations. For a heterogeneity amplitude of $H=0.8$ and a correlation length of $\xi=3\,\mu\mathrm{m}$, the crossover occurs at approximately $1.50\times10^{12}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$, while the ensemble relative dose variance approaches a plateau of $0.160$ at high fluence. Boron heterogeneity also increases the probability that a nucleus receives no energy deposition from alpha--lithium reaction products. At $\xi=6\,\mu\mathrm{m}$ and $\Phi_n=3\times10^{11}\,\mathrm{cm}^{-2}$, the zero-hit probability is $40.49\%$ higher than that for a homogeneous boron distribution with the same mean concentration. This study shows that spatial boron correlations and stochastic neutron capture influence nuclear dose fluctuations and zero-hit statistics beyond what can be characterized by mean boron concentration alone.
item.dc:creator: Ramacos Fardela, Roni Muslim, Tista Artu Indra Kusuma

item.title: A Cracked Mirror: How People Perceive Gender Performance by Large Language Models
item.description: arXiv:2611.06393v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: How do large language models (LLMs) perform gender under zero-shot prompting, and how do people interpret those performances in conversation? Drawing on gender performativity, we examine how gendered meanings emerge through generated language, conversational context and human interpretation. In a preregistered randomised online experiment, 1,060 participants each had five short conversations with an LLM. We used minimal prompts to elicit performances from "very masculine" to "very feminine" and asked participants to rate their partner's perceived gender after each conversation. Mean ratings shifted in the direction of the prompts, but ratings at the extremes were closer to the midpoint than the prompt labels implied. When prompted to perform as "neither masculine nor feminine", the models were perceived as slightly masculine on average. Ratings varied across models and conversation topics. Women and men gave similar ratings at the extremes, but women rated the models as more masculine across the intermediate prompt levels. Participants' explanations illustrate how they drew on writing style, emotional expression and conversational interests, sometimes questioning the stereotypes behind their judgements. These findings suggest that conversational AI acts as a cracked mirror of gender norms. Models reproduce recognisable cues, and people interpret and sometimes challenge the meanings those cues carry.
item.dc:creator: Faezeh Fadaei, Jenny Carla Moran, Taha Yasseri

item.title: Emergent regularity of walking patterns: evidence from Swiss cities
item.description: arXiv:2611.06529v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Human travel behaviour is characterised by high temporal and spatial regularity, as demonstrated by the Exploration and Preferential Return (EPR) mechanism, whereby individuals alternate between exploring new locations and preferentially returning to previously visited places. Yet, existing evidence is based on aggregated mobility data that cannot distinguish short trips or separate active mobility (i.e., walking and biking) from other mobility modes. This limits our ability to assess the benefits of walking activities and proximity-based policies such as the 15-minute city. Here, we analyse the spatial distribution and duration of walking habits of 1,318 participants, tracked during a 4-week time use survey in major Swiss cities - which are very close to the 15-minute city model. We find that walking activity is highly concentrated around individuals' home and work locations. These two attractors create walking patterns that are fundamentally different from other transport modes, which are instead used for longer trips and to connect home-workplace. We then introduce a dual-center EPR model, with empirically derived parameters, to simulate the decaying probability of walking away from the centers. Combining empirical data and the EPR framework, we find that groups with higher walking times show a stronger tendency to take long-distance walks and explore more destinations. In general, walking behavior reflects both individual circumstances and residential context: walking durations are shorter among people without a public transport pass, car owners, and residents of low-density rural areas. These findings provide a basis for more targeted assessments of walkability and active-mobility-oriented urban design.
item.dc:creator: Guo-Shiuan Lin, Martin Hendrick, Maider Llaguno-Munitxa, Gabriele Manoli

item.title: Informing research priorities for distributed acoustic sensing: insights from a citizens' panel
item.description: arXiv:2611.06584v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: This report presents findings from a Citizens' Panel convened by the SOUNDSCALE project (www.soundscale.ac.uk) to inform research priorities for distributed acoustic sensing (DAS). Across three online and in-person workshops, 48 residents from Hampshire and London explored the technology's potential uses, risks, governance, and societal implications. The report summarises their deliberations and priorities, and reflects on the challenges of involving citizens in early-stage research on an unfamiliar technology.
item.dc:creator: Hannah Dalgleish, Rafael Mestre, Heidi Wheatley, Angela YT Chan, Mariya Yanishevskaya, Duncan Grimes, Sophie Hart, Sergey Astakhov, Matt Ryan, Dianna Smith, Alexandra Anikina, Ceri Davies-Tyrie, Gianluca Audone, Mohammad Belal, Louis Cook

item.title: Limited knowledge exchange across biological subfields in agent-based modelling: an LLM-assisted bibliometric analysis
item.description: arXiv:2611.06596v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: Agent-based models (ABMs) are widely used across the biological sciences. While applications differ between biological subfields, the mathematical and statistical methods underlying ABMs largely do not, raising the question of how much knowledge is exchanged between subfields. We address this question by developing a bibliometric pipeline that combines a database keyword search with coarse- and fine-grained classification by a large language model (LLM). We apply the pipeline to the Web of Science Core Collection, classifying 22,936 ABM articles into ecology, epidemiology, oncology, other-biology, or not-biology. Using citation patterns and author overlap as proxies for knowledge exchange, we find that 83%, 81%, and 69% of citations from ecology, epidemiology, and oncology articles, respectively, go to articles in the same subfield. Furthermore, 91% of authors with at least two articles across these subfields publish exclusively within one subfield. Both proportions far exceed those expected under random assignment of subfields (permutation tests, $p \leq 0.001$). Terminology also differs, with "individual-based model" used mainly in ecology and "agent-based model" in epidemiology, oncology, and outside biology. Taken together, our results suggest limited knowledge exchange between biological subfields in ABM research, leading us to discuss opportunities for increased exchange through conferences, journals, and training.
item.dc:creator: Kira Pugh, Rebecca M Crossley, Sara Hamis

item.title: How Rich is the Rich-Club? Super Rich-Club Organization in Complex Networks
item.description: arXiv:2611.06756v1 Announce Type: new Abstract: The rich-club coefficient is used in complex networks to quantify the tendency of progressively higher-degree nodes to be more densely connected than expected by chance. However, it does not capture whether high degree nodes towards the core are actually more interconnected than the original network. Here, we jointly analyze the rich-club coefficient and an enrichment coefficient, which quantifies whether the internal average degree of progressively higher-degree subgraphs is greater than that of the original network, despite the decreasing number of nodes. We apply this framework to real and synthetic networks. Our results reveal three distinct regimes of core organization: rich-club organization without enrichment, enrichment without rich-club organization, and a combination of both, which we call Super Rich-Club organization. In the latter regime, high-degree nodes form cohesive and unusually dense cores that support efficient communication. Our results show that characterizing core organization across structural scales requires considering both relative density and internal connectivity, revealing a stronger form of core organization in real systems with implications for network structure, spectral properties that govern dynamical processes, and communicability.
item.dc:creator: Luc\'ia S. Ramirez, Laia Barjuan, M. \'Angeles Serrano

item.title: Phase Locking in Oscillator Networks with Uncertain and State-Dependent Couplings
item.description: arXiv:2611.06466v1 Announce Type: cross Abstract: Phase locking in oscillator networks depends critically on the interaction strengths between coupled units. In many applications, however, these couplings are uncertain, state dependent, or time varying. We derive rigorous conditions for phase locking in Kuramoto-type networks when each coupling strength is known only within prescribed bounds. Building on a convex formulation of the nonlinear fixed-point equations, we obtain edge-wise error bounds for arbitrary feasible approximations that hold uniformly over all admissible couplings. These bounds yield sufficient conditions for the existence of phase-locked states with prescribed phase-difference limits. We illustrate the framework for AC power grids with uncertain voltage magnitudes and adaptive oscillator networks with state-dependent couplings. For the latter, the bounds can be further tightened by exploiting the state dependence of the couplings.
item.dc:creator: Iva Ba\v{c}i\'c, Philipp C. B\"ottcher, Marc Hunkem\"oller, Carsten Hartmann, David Gross, Andrea Benigni, Dirk Witthaut

item.title: A self-organizing mechanism for collective foraging: recruitment cascades couple Levy search to a clustered maximum-entropy resource field
item.description: arXiv:2610.24865v4 Announce Type: replace Abstract: Foraging recruitment is modeled as a contagion: an agent that finds a resource triggers a linear-threshold cascade on the group's communication network. Because activation is degree-normalized, crowding shuts the cascade off, so the swarm aggregates on a resource and then disperses to explore again. Acting on the cascade moves agents in space, and that motion rewires the network, so recruitment and exploration are one coupled process; removing this coupling alone abolishes the self-limitation. Recruitment spreads only within a connectivity window, bounded below by percolation onset and above by degree-blocking. The swarm self-organizes to the near-critical edge of this window -- self-organized quasi-criticality: recruitment sits near but below the critical point without settling onto a clean, size-invariant critical state, and the activity spectrum has a finite correlation time (Lorentzian-like, not 1/f), consistent with local rather than global criticality. Recruitment raises harvest up to 2.7x over solitary search on sparse, clustered resource fields and loses (down to 0.37x) on abundant or uniform ones; because resources generically aggregate, the favourable regime is the common one. The empirically motivated Levy search and the resource field it exploits are both least-committal: the search a maximum-caliber walk, and the field a maximum-entropy point process whose generic, aggregation-set sign is clustered (attractive). The search exponent that maximizes harvest tracks the field's fractal dimension (a heavier-tailed, more ballistic search for more strongly clustered fields). These are one coupled mechanism: heavy-tailed Levy exploration crosses the field's sparse voids while recruitment cascades exploit its clusters, so one maximum-entropy geometry binds exploration and recruitment into a single self-organizing cycle.
item.dc:creator: Galen J. Wilkerson
